A table scores three requested pairs by shared over total distinct neighbors: B, E is 2 of 5 = 0.4, C, D is 2 of 3 = 0.67, and A, E is 0." width="100%"} For each pair of nodes `(u, v)`, computes `|N(u) ∩ N(v)| / |N(u) ∪ N(v)|`, which is the ratio of common neighbors to total distinct neighbors. The score lies in `[0, 1]`: `1` means the two nodes have exactly the same neighbors and `0` means they share none. The graph is not modified. Compared with a raw `common_neighbors()` count, the Jaccard coefficient accounts for how many neighbors each node has, so a pair of hubs that happen to share a few neighbors does not automatically outrank a pair of small nodes that share all of theirs. It is useful for: - link prediction where node degrees vary widely - measuring structural similarity (overlap of neighborhoods) between two nodes - finding near-duplicate or redundant nodes (scores close to `1`) The measure is intended for undirected graphs. On a directed graph, neighbors are the *outgoing* neighbors. When `ebunch=` is `None`, every pair of non-adjacent nodes is scored, which is quadratic in the number of nodes; pass `ebunch=` on large graphs. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ebunch]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [list[tuple[Union[int, str], Union[int, str]]]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : List of `(u, v)` node pairs to score. Each node can be given as a node ID (`int`) or label (`str`). Pairs are scored even if `u` and `v` are already connected, and they are returned in the order given. If `None` (the default), all pairs of nodes that are not already connected (in either direction) are scored, each unordered pair once, in no particular order. A node that doesn't exist raises a `ValueError`. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [list[tuple[int, int, float]]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : List of `(u, v, coefficient)` tuples where coefficient is the Jaccard similarity. Nodes are reported as node IDs. Coefficient is `0.0` if both nodes have no neighbors. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If a node in `ebunch=` does not exist in the graph. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} The Jaccard coefficient normalizes common neighbors by the total distinct neighbors of the two nodes: $J(u, v) = \dfrac{|N(u) \cap N(v)|}{|N(u) \cup N(v)|} \in [0, 1]$, with $1$ signalling identical neighborhoods and $0$ meaning no overlap. The normalization makes it fairer than raw common-neighbor counts when comparing pairs with very different degrees, at the cost of inflating scores for low-degree pairs (two isolated leaves that share their only neighbor score a perfect $1$). Cost is $O(k)$ per pair. ## Examples {.doc-examples} On a 5-node path `1-2-3-4-5`, nodes `1` and `3` share neighbor `2` out of two distinct neighbors (`2` and `4`), giving `0.5`. Nodes `2` and `4` share only `3` out of `{1, 3, 5}`, giving `1/3`, and `1` and `4` share nothing: ::: {#d245a35d .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ec.Graph(directed=False) graph.add_path_graph(5) # 1-2-3-4-5 graph.jaccard_coefficient([(1, 3), (1, 4), (2, 4)]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` [(1, 3, 0.5), (1, 4, 0.0), (2, 4, 0.3333333333333333)] ``` ::: ::: Normalization changes the ranking compared with raw counts. Below, `Hub1` and `Hub2` share two neighbors but each also has two the other lacks, while the leaves `Lee` and `Max` each have a single neighbor, and it is the same one. Common neighbors favors the hubs (2 vs. 1); Jaccard favors the leaves (`1.0` vs. `2/6`, about `0.33`): ::: {#0bf109ab .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ec.Graph(directed=False) graph.add_nodes(["Hub1", "Hub2", "A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F", "Lee", "Max"]) graph.add_edges( [ ("Hub1", "A"), ("Hub1", "B"), ("Hub1", "C"), ("Hub1", "D"), ("Hub2", "A"), ("Hub2", "B"), ("Hub2", "E"), ("Hub2", "F"), ("Lee", "C"), ("Max", "C"), ] ) pairs = [("Hub1", "Hub2"), ("Lee", "Max")] [ (cn[2], round(jc[2], 2)) for cn, jc in zip(graph.common_neighbors(pairs), graph.jaccard_coefficient(pairs)) ] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` [(2, 0.33), (1, 1.0)] ``` ::: :::
